title: Hurricane Isaias live updates: hundreds of thousands without power as storm batters US Gulf Coast
summary: First Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season makes landfall in the US

blocks.text: More than 860,000 without power
Isaias has left more than 860,000 people without electricity as it moves inland across the south-east.
Here’s the latest breakdown of the worst affected states, according to poweroutage.us:
Florida: 436,745
Alabama: 316,366
Georgia: 87,334
Washington: 6,550
California: 4,467
Texas: 4,404
Ohio: 3,827
Idaho: 1,549

blocks.caption: People look at wind, rain, and flying debris from a hotel lobby in Pensacola, Florida, during a power outage ahead of the arrival of hurricane Isaias. Photograph: Marco Bello/Reuters

blocks.text: Isaias, first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season, batters US Gulf coast
More than half a million people were without power after hurricane Isaias wreaked havoc on the US Gulf Coast, with Alabama and the Florida Panhandle being hit the hardest by the storm.

The category 2 hurricane made landfall near Destin, Florida, late Friday, with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour. It weakened to a post-tropical cyclone by early morning, with winds of 65 mph, the National Weather Service said.

blocks.caption: Debris is seen in an intersection in Pensacola, Florida as wind and rain from Hurricane Isaias pass through the area. Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images

blocks.text: More than 750,000 people in Florida and Alabama have been left without power, according to poweroutage.us, with outages also reported in Georgia for tens of thousands of customers.

“Things are flying really fast, and I’ve never seen wind this fast before, so it’s intense, it’s scary,” Jonathan Ramos, a 40-year-old government employee, said from his hotel in Pensacola, Florida, where the power went out.
“I don’t recommend people coming down here for fun to do this.”

Isaias intensified into a hurricane on Wednesday night, then becoming the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.

In the days prior to landfall, storm surge warnings were in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwannee River in Florida. Residents in the affected areas were urged to follow advice from local officials and evacuate if instructed to do so.
